dailyRead: This week ended with the thing this file has been describing for four sessions finally being named by the tape: the Dow and the S&P 500 both closed in correction, more than 10% below their highs, and the Nasdaq Composite gave back every point of its 2026 gain. The numbers are worth stating precisely because the scale is what changes the FX read. The Dow fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33. The S&P 500 fell 3.7% to 6,910.39 and is 8.6% lower on the week. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.28% to 22,617.73. The Nasdaq-100 fell 5.61% to 25,028.98 and traded in bear-market territory intraday. On the futures Darius trades the week was worse still: YM finished 8.01% lower on the week and NQ 11.52% lower, with NQ printing 24,977 at its low. Nvidia closed down 14.01% at 125.53 dollars, its worst single session since January 2025, after Reuters reported that SEC enforcement staff are examining potential accounting issues at the company - roughly 500 billion dollars of market value in one day, on top of the Wall Street Journal report on November 17 that the SEC was looking at whether its disclosures misled investors, a California investigative subpoena issued on November 19 and the resignation of Jensen Huang as chief executive on November 12. AMD and Broadcom each fell more than 13%. That matters for the analysis because it changes what kind of shock this is. Up to Thursday the honest description was an AI derating inside a hawkish-Fed regime. Friday made it something narrower and more dangerous: a single-name accounting and governance event at the largest position in the index, transmitting through the whole AI complex. And the bond market agreed it was not about rates. The US 10-year fell about 11 basis points to 4.944% from 5.04%, its fifth consecutive decline and its first close under 5% in some time, with the 30-year at 5.31% and the 2-year at 4.698%, and traders backed away from the fifty-point December bet. December is still about 97.3% priced for a quarter point on CME FedWatch - Philadelphia Fed President Paulson said again on Friday that another increase is needed - but the tail that was doing the damage has gone. So the two things that are supposed to support the dollar, a hawkish Fed and a global growth scare, were both present on Friday and the dollar still lost 0.71% to the yen and 0.49% to the franc. DXY closed at 103.840, down 0.05%, still inside its 19-month-high region but 2.02% lower over four weeks. That is now the fourth consecutive session in which hawkish news has failed to pay in the dollar, and it is the single most actionable fact on this board: the trades with an edge are the ones that do not need a dollar leg. Where the dollar did win was against the two commodity currencies, 0.44% against the Australian dollar and 0.24% against the kiwi, which is the correct expression of a growth shock and the reason the book is tilted that way rather than being short the dollar outright. The yen is the clean winner and goes to plus three. It rose against all seven others for a second straight session - 0.71% on USD/JPY to 158.554, 1.17% on AUD/JPY to 105.087, 0.95% on NZD/JPY, 0.74% on GBP/JPY, 0.72% on both EUR/JPY and CAD/JPY and 0.24% on CHF/JPY - and it did so with the US yield leg finally moving in its favour. A yen that rallies on the day its own CPI misses on all three measures is a haven bid; a yen that rallies while the US 10-year drops 11 basis points is a haven bid with the carry leg narrowing behind it, which is a different and better trade. The policy case is intact underneath: the policy rate is 1.25%, TradingEconomics carries 1.50% for December 18, December is priced somewhere between 78% and 85%, 61 of 71 economists polled expect the move, wage growth is 4.6% and core CPI at 2.2% has now been above target for a second month. The franc takes second place and moves to plus two: it gained against six of the seven, beaten only by the yen, with USD/CHF down 0.49% to 0.83986 and AUD/CHF down 0.98%. The Swiss National Bank sits at 0.00% with headline inflation at 1.5% that is almost entirely imported energy, core at 0.5% and a near-certain hold on December 10, so the franc has no policy story at all - its only driver is the haven bid, and its only cap is the bank's standing readiness to sell francs, which is exactly why it does the junior version of whatever the yen does. The euro keeps plus one and the forward case got stronger again: December 17 pricing has moved up to roughly 96% to 96.8%, from about 91% on Thursday and the 67% to 84% range of a week ago, with the deposit facility rate at 2.50%, HICP at a three-year high of 4.0%, core at 2.6% and rising - and the input behind that print accelerating hard, with EU natural gas up 6.02% in a single session to 89.54 euros on an outage at the Troll field and lower Norwegian exports, now 196.52% higher than a year ago. The euro did not get paid for it on the day, which is why the backward verdict stays mixed while the forward is hawkish, but it beat sterling, the Canadian dollar and both antipodeans and was flat against the dollar. The dollar comes down a notch to plus one for the reasons above. Sterling stays at zero: Bank Rate is 4.00% after the November 5 hike on an 8-1 vote, CPI is 3.6% with core steady at 2.8%, unemployment improved to 4.6%, and December 17 remains the most genuinely two-sided decision on the board - market pricing between 74% and 80% against all but one of 65 economists polled by Reuters expecting a hold, with coverage on Friday still calling it finely balanced and February the consensus for the next move. The kiwi comes down to minus one, and the honest statement is that the leg which broke is the price, not the policy. The December 9 Monetary Policy Statement still carries 3.00% against the current 2.75% on TradingEconomics own calendar and that is still the only move outside the Fed, ECB and Bank of Japan that this board is carrying, but after two sessions as the best-performing non-haven the kiwi fell against six of seven and only beat the Australian dollar, by 0.10%. Canada stays at minus two. One session of oil going the right way does not repair it: WTI rose 1.43% to 83.62 and Brent 0.63% to 92.56, but WTI is still 13.93% lower on the month, which is the removal of the exact pass-through the October hike was aimed at, and core CPI at 2.0%, trimmed at 1.8% and median at 2.0% are all at or below the midpoint with unemployment at 6.7% and three consecutive monthly employment falls. The disagreement that makes USD/CAD the most exposed position here is unchanged and now has a date: TradingEconomics own calendar forecasts a rise to 2.75% on December 9 while the rate market prices about 38%, and Governor Macklem speaks on Tuesday at 18:30, which is the first real test of which of those two is right. The Australian dollar stays at minus three and at the bottom. It fell against all seven others. Both of its legs are broken and neither is close to mending: October employment fell 43,500 against a plus 25,500 forecast with unemployment at a four-year high of 4.9%, which removes any case for a hike, while headline inflation at 4.3% and core at 3.6% - the highest on this board - removes any case for a cut, leaving a central bank frozen at 4.85% into December 8; and the terms-of-trade leg went with copper, down another 3.04% to 5.46 dollars a pound and 16.52% lower on the month. The October CPI print on Wednesday at 02:30 is the week's only chance to change that, and it is the one event that could force the board to pick a side. The metals need their own paragraph because this is where the regime shows itself most clearly. Gold fell 2.51% to 3,535 dollars, a 14-month low, 14.64% lower on the month and down roughly 9% on the week, its worst week in about eight months. Silver fell 3.86% to 41.19 and is 28.93% lower on the month. Both fell on a day when the US 10-year dropped 11 basis points. That is not a real-rate trade and it is not a view change - a metal that falls while its primary driver moves in its favour is being sold by someone who has to sell, and the coverage describing margin calls and fund redemptions is the correct explanation. The consequence for the book is that gold loses its directional edge here rather than gaining one: 3,500 is a round number sitting immediately below, the liquidation signature says the move ends somewhere near it rather than accelerating through it, and so XAU/USD becomes a range to trade rather than a short to press. Silver keeps a direction because it has a second leg that is genuinely still breaking, which is the industrial one, and copper at 16.52% lower on the month is that leg. Europe's equity indices fell with everything else and the interesting detail is which fell more: the EU50 lost 3.06% to 5,937 while the DAX lost 2.60% to 24,803. That is the opposite of what a hawkish-ECB tape alone would produce, because banks are the heaviest sector in the EU50 and a near-certain December hike with a steepening curve should be helping that weight. It did not, which says the global derating and the French political and credit overhang - S&P reviews France on Friday - are dominating the bank leg rather than being offset by it. The DAX carries its own distinct problem in gas at 89.54 euros and plus 6.02%, which is a direct input cost rather than a sentiment question. Oil remains the one place where the story has not changed at all. Day 265 of the closure. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported an outbound tanker hit by an unknown projectile on Friday eight nautical miles north of Khasab in Oman's Musandam region, with a fire aboard and no casualties; Iran's army again claimed oil tankers struck naval mines east of the strait, without evidence, while the United States says the southern lanes near Oman have been cleared of mines; US forces struck an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps missile site on Qeshm Island, which Iran said caused no serious damage; and Iran's navy repeated that the strait is closed. Against all that, WTI rose 1.43% and is 13.93% lower on the month, the IEA projects a global surplus near 2 million barrels a day, the US, China and Russia agreed on Thursday to boost refined product supply, and the US Energy Secretary says flows through the strait have reached record levels. A market that will not bid a tanker fire has no premium left to unwind, so the asymmetry points up while the trend points down and USOIL stays a range. The week ahead is short and lopsided. Flash PMIs on Monday for Germany at 10:30, the euro area at 11:00, the UK at 11:30 and the US at 16:45, with Fed's Williams, ECB's Lane and the Bank of England's Pill speaking. Macklem on Tuesday at 18:30 and US consumer confidence at 17:00. Then everything lands at once on Wednesday: Australian CPI at 02:30 and US October core PCE with the second estimate of Q3 GDP at 15:30, core forecast unchanged at 0.3% m/m and rising to 3.2% y/y, headline at 3.8% from 3.6%. Thursday is Thanksgiving with the New York Stock Exchange and the bond market closed, Tokyo CPI arrives at 01:30 Bucharest on Friday, and Friday is an early US close at 20:00 with the S&P review of France in the evening. Two things follow from that shape. The first is that Wednesday carries essentially the entire week's information in a single 15:30 print, eleven days before a meeting where the fifty-point tail has just been priced out and could be priced straight back in. The second is that from Wednesday afternoon the tape is thin, and a thin tape in a market that has just entered a correction is how gaps happen in both directions - which is an argument for taking the yen and franc crosses, where the edge is a score gap of four or five rather than one, and for sizing down everything that depends on the dollar picking a side.

catalysts.event: The AI derating becomes a single-name accounting event

geopolitics: The inversion this file has described all week survived its hardest test yet and is now better evidenced than it was. Day 265 of the closure. On Friday the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported an outbound tanker struck by an unknown projectile eight nautical miles north of Khasab in Oman's Musandam region, with a fire aboard and no casualties or environmental impact; US forces hit an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps missile site on Qeshm Island in what a US official described as self-defence, with an Iranian regional official saying the strikes caused no serious damage; Iran's army again claimed oil tankers caught fire after striking naval mines in a restricted area east of the strait, a claim it has repeated for weeks without evidence; and Iran's navy repeated that the strait is closed. The United States says the southern shipping lanes close to Oman's coast have been cleared of mines, and the US Energy Secretary says flows through the strait have reached record levels - those two statements and Iran's are not reconcilable, so the physical figures should be read as contested estimates rather than facts, which is how they are treated here. Against all of that, WTI rose 1.43% to 83.62 dollars and Brent 0.63% to 92.56, and WTI is still 13.93% lower on the month with Brent 14.94% lower. The reason is on the supply side and it is specific: the IEA projects a global surplus near 2 million barrels a day, and the United States, China and Russia agreed at a trilateral meeting on Thursday to boost the production and supply of refined petroleum products. A market that will not bid a tanker fire has no premium left to unwind, so the direction of the asymmetry is up while the direction of the trend is down, and USOIL stays a range rather than a short. What has changed this week, and changed decisively on Friday, is that oil is no longer the dominant cross-asset story. The AI derating is, and it stopped being a theme and became an event. Reuters reported that SEC enforcement staff are examining potential accounting issues at Nvidia; the stock fell 14.01% to 125.53 dollars, its worst single session since January 2025, losing roughly 500 billion dollars of market value in a day, on top of the Wall Street Journal report of November 17 on whether its disclosures misled investors, a California investigative subpoena on November 19 and Jensen Huang's resignation as chief executive on November 12. AMD and Broadcom each fell more than 13%. The index consequences were the Dow closing 1.93% lower at 48,147.33 and the S&P 500 3.7% lower at 6,910.39, both more than 10% below their highs and therefore formally in correction, the Nasdaq Composite falling 5.28% to 22,617.73 to erase its entire 2026 gain, and the Nasdaq-100 falling 5.61% to 25,028.98 after trading in bear-market territory intraday. On the futures the week closed with YM 8.01% lower and NQ 11.52% lower. This matters for currencies because it fixes the character of the shock. It is a growth-and-credit shock with a governance accelerant, not a rates shock - and the bond market said so by rallying: the US 10-year fell about 11 basis points to 4.944% from 5.04%, its fifth consecutive decline, with the 2-year at 4.698% and the 30-year at 5.31%, and traders backed away from the fifty-point December bet while leaving the quarter point near 97.3%. That is why gold fell 2.51% to a 14-month low of 3,535 on a day its primary driver moved in its favour, why silver fell 3.86% and is 28.93% lower on the month, and why copper lost another 3.04% to 5.46 and is 16.52% lower on the month. Metals falling alongside equities while real rates improve is the signature of forced selling, and the coverage describing margin calls and fund redemptions is the correct explanation rather than a view change. The transmission into the eight currencies is clean and it is the whole basis of today's book. The yen is the primary beneficiary and goes to plus three because the trade improved in kind: it rose against all seven others for a second session, and this time the US carry leg narrowed behind it rather than fighting it. The franc takes the junior share at plus two, up against six of seven, capped only by the Swiss National Bank's standing readiness to sell francs - which is precisely why the yen crosses get high conviction and the franc crosses get medium. The Australian dollar is the primary casualty at minus three, because copper is its terms-of-trade leg and the AI capex unwind is removing it on top of a four-year-high unemployment rate and a central bank frozen at 4.85%. The kiwi comes down to minus one: its December 9 hike is still carried at 3.00% with a full forecast round, but after two sessions of outperformance it lost to six of seven, so the policy leg survived and the price leg did not. Canada holds minus two deliberately - one session of crude rising 1.43% does not repair a thesis built on a 13.93% monthly fall, both preferred cores at or below the midpoint and three consecutive employment falls - but Macklem on Tuesday at 18:30 is the first real test of TradingEconomics 2.75% December forecast against the market's 38%. Europe is still the only place where the oil conflict pays through inflation rather than through growth: EU natural gas rose 6.02% in a single session to 89.54 euros on an outage at the Troll gas field and lower Norwegian exports, and is 196.52% higher than a year ago, so the euro area keeps the inflation cost of the conflict without any terms-of-trade relief - which is exactly what holds HICP at a three-year high of 4.0% and has pushed December 17 pricing to 96.0% to 96.8% in two upward steps. The dollar remains the surprise and it is now a four-session pattern rather than an observation. It should be the second beneficiary of a global growth scare and it is not: DXY closed 103.840 and minus 0.05%, lower by 0.71% against the yen and 0.49% against the franc on the day two US indices entered correction, and 2.02% lower over four weeks. Four consecutive hawkish catalysts have produced no dollar gain, and on Friday the yield cushion thinned as well. That moves the dollar from strengthening to mixed and makes the single most actionable statement on this board the same one as yesterday, only stronger: the trades with an edge are the ones that do not need a dollar leg. Where the dollar did win was against the Australian dollar and the kiwi, which is the correct expression of a growth shock and the reason the book is tilted that way rather than being short the dollar outright. Looking forward, the scenario that re-prices everything at once on the oil side is still a confirmed physical supply interruption rather than another contested claim: WTI through 95 would restore the Canadian inflation argument and terms of trade together, invert the USD/CAD long and force the European growth-versus-inflation trade-off back toward growth. Nothing in the current price pays for that. The scenario that re-prices everything on the rates side is much closer and has a time on it: US October core PCE on Wednesday at 15:30. A core print of 0.4% m/m or more puts the fifty-point tail straight back, and with it the dollar, while taking gold through 3,500 and both indices to new lows. A soft core leaves the correction as the only story in a market that then has to trade it through a Thanksgiving week with no US cash session on Thursday and an early close on Friday - thin, headline-sensitive and gap-prone in both directions, which is the practical argument for size in the yen and franc crosses, where the score gap is four or five points, and for small size in everything that needs the dollar to finally pick a side.
